moves.spoken: White again, and against the Sicilian we stick with what has been working — the Alapin.
The quiet c3.
Black plays e6.
White grabs the centre with d4.
Black plays a6 — the same passive treatment as the previous opponent.
White clamps down with d5, seizing a big space advantage.
Black bolts the centre with d6.
White develops the knight to f3.
Black locks it up further with e5 — a closed, cramped structure with almost no room to breathe.
White develops the bishop to d3.
Black plays h6 — the previous opponent went for the bishop to g4; this one tucks the pawn in first.
White develops the queen's knight to d2.

Black lunges with g5, trying to intimidate. But the question to ask is which weaknesses g5 has created — and immediately you should spot the f5 square, exactly the theme from the last game. So the plan is the same: reroute a knight, to g3 or e3, and steer it toward f5.
White plays the knight to f1. There is no bishop to chase off here, but the target is still that f5 square.
Black rams the pawn on to g4.
And now a striking move — the knight all the way back to g1. Retreating is badly misunderstood, but the goal is to reach f5, and this is the first step of the journey.
Black keeps rolling with h5.
The knight comes to e3 — two goals now: to get a knight to f5, and to prise the position open, since Black has pushed nothing but pawns.
Black develops the knight to e7.
Now the point of that retreat reveals itself — the g1-knight supports h3, cracking open the h-file toward the king.
Black takes on h3.
And the knight redeploys to h3. Knights on the rim are grim, they say — but this one has a bright future via g5, and the position is cracking open thanks to Black's woeful development.
Black brings a knight to g6.

And there it is — the other knight lands on f5, the second goal achieved. Black can take it, but White recaptures with the pawn, chases the knight, and may even ram the pawn to f6. Normally you want to recapture an outpost with a piece — but White is so dominant in development that keeping the flames roaring matters more.
Black finally develops the bishop to e7. Now White starts hunting for the kill — there is a loose, undefended pawn to snatch, right where the pieces make contact.

The knight checks from g7, drives the king to f8, and snaps off the h-pawn — pawn-grabbing White would normally avoid, but total domination makes it fine, and it rips the h-file wide open. Who knows, maybe one day mate arrives down that file.
Black lunges with the knight to h4, and it looks threatening — but White can shut it down without even defending.
White simply plays g3. The check on g2 holds no fear — the knight would trap itself; it has to slink back to g6.

Back it slinks to g6. Now White brings the queen out to x-ray the king, develops the bishop, and castles long to link the rooks — finally ready to storm the kingside, with the whole plan bearing down the open h-file.
A clean game — Black did much of the work himself.
The whole game turned on g5 — it weakened the f5 square permanently, and that is what made this plan so strong.
And now the retreat to g1 should make sense — a piece is not bad simply for sitting on an ugly square; judge it by its role. This one's role was to prepare h3 and rip open the h-file toward the king.

Being down material is fine if what you have is Messi-level material. A knight is not bad for sitting on g1; it has a very specific job — so judge a piece by the role it fills, not by how many squares it happens to cover.
Why the detour to g1 at all — why not just play h3 at once? Because right now h3 is met by the bishop, the file stays shut, and you only weaken your own king for nothing.

There is a second point: if h3 never comes off, the knight can instead reroute to g3 and pair with its partner on e3, both covering f5. Sometimes you must step back to go forward — the most famous example is Nimzowitsch's knight to h1 against Rubinstein in 1926, the knight travelling all the way around to g5, through ugly squares, to find the fountain of youth.
How do you know when a slow, many-move plan is justified? Judgment — and here it is justified because Black has pushed only pawns and simply lacks the firepower to punish the time spent.
